chapters.file: ch15 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Baltzer-Jaray uses Kant's phenomena/noumena split, Plato's Forms, and Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to ask whether Jack Skellington can know the essence of Christmas and whether Vincent Malloy can know what it is to BE Vincent Price. She argues Jack's lab-experiments on presents and snowflakes ('Jack's Obsession') can only yield phenomena, never the noumenal essence, so Kant would permit belief but not knowledge; Vincent, watching only Price's horror roles, grasps a mere phenomenal fragment. Via Nagel she concludes neither can occupy another's subjective viewpoint, so the lesson of both films is to celebrate otherness through communication rather than trying to be someone else.

chapters.file: ch16 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
ch17 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Jenkins reads Burton's 'Sweeney Todd' (2007) through Edmund Burke's theory of the sublime and the device of synesthesia. She argues Burton relocates Burke's sublime from nature to the man-made, consuming city, staging beauty (Johanna, the flower-market flashbacks, saturated color) in losing tension with the 'dark and gloomy' urban sublime (desaturated Fleet Street, 'Epiphany'). Drawing on German Expressionist visual style (Caligari, Nosferatu) and the raindrop-to-blood credit sequence, she shows how sight, sound and represented taste (Mrs. Lovett's cannibal pies, the jugular-spray 'shooting star' during 'Johanna') mix the senses to force the queasy Burkean confrontation of terror and delight, ending in Burke's nihilistic darkness rather than redemption.

chapters.file: ch18 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Knight and McKnight apply Tzvetan Todorov's categories of 'the fantastic,' 'the uncanny,' and 'the marvelous' to the eight Burton films starring Johnny Depp, arguing that Burton treats the fantastic not as a genre but as a transgeneric film MODE that sustains the viewer's hesitation between natural and supernatural explanation. Using Wayne Booth's notion of the authorial 'second self,' they cast Depp as Burton's persona/surrogate who realizes and sustains that uncertainty (Edward, Ed Wood, Ichabod Crane, Willy Wonka, Sweeney, the Hatter). They classify 'Ed Wood' and 'Edward Scissorhands' as resolving into the uncanny (rationally explicable) and 'Sleepy Hollow,' 'Corpse Bride,' 'Alice in Wonderland,' and 'Dark Shadows' as passing into the marvelous, where new laws of nature must be accepted.

chapters.file: ch19 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: McMahon argues Burton's death-saturated corpus functions as modern memento mori that fosters Heideggerian authenticity by arousing the uncanny and honest awareness of being-toward-death. She supplements Freud's account of the unheimliche (which she says wrongly substitutes castration anxiety for the primal fear of death) with Heidegger's link of angst, uncanniness, and finitude in 'Being and Time,' plus Terror Management Theory. Reading 'The Nightmare Before Christmas,' 'Corpse Bride,' and 'Dark Shadows,' she shows Jack, Bonejangles's Dance of Death, Emily, and vampire Barnabas use animation, comedy, and romance to make death palatable, and contrasts these films with Nozick's escapist experience machine—Burton supplements reality rather than replacing it.

chapters.file: ch20 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: LaRocca argues Burton's 'Ed Wood' (1994) is a metafilm that, via Baudrillard's simulacra and Plato's cave/dialectic, transforms how we watch Wood's 'bad' films. He casts Wood as a cave-dweller and naive literalist who conflates representation with reality ('film equals life,' 'that was perfect'), while Burton is the Platonic dialectician who posits two worlds and provokes thought. He distinguishes two interacting metafilm types—biographical simulacrum (a hyperreal Ed Wood with no original, per Baudrillard's 'artificial resurrection') and mimetic reenactment (loyal remakes of Wood's films)—so that Martin Landau's Lugosi and Parker-as-Fuller's non-acting reveal the emotional 'affect without illusion' latent in Wood's work.

chapters.file: ch21 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Olson argues Burton's signature saturated-versus-drab color palette in 'The Nightmare Before Christmas' and 'Corpse Bride' operates as a marketing strategy that commodifies childhood, conditioning children as future consumers who associate the films' colors with a utopian fantasy world to be bought back. She reads Jack's craving for the color of Christmas Town ('I want it for my own') through Lacan's objet petit a and through bell hooks's 'commodification of difference' (the Other consumed while its meaning is stripped away), and treats the Disney/Burton fairy-tale film as a Fordist commodity whose color palette—echoed on store shelves—drives product loyalty and nostalgic desire.

holes.name: Edmund Burke
holes.what: 18th-century thinker whose 'Philosophical Enquiry' theorizes the sublime as awe born of terror-at-a-distance, opposed to beauty.
holes.why: Chapter 17's entire argument about 'Sweeney Todd' is built on Burke's aesthetics of the sublime, and no philosopher slug for Burke exists in the taxonomy.

holes.name: The Sublime
holes.what: The aesthetic experience of overwhelming awe blending pain, terror, and delight, set in opposition to beauty.
holes.why: Chapter 17 applies the sublime (and its tension with beauty) to Burton's urban 'Sweeney Todd' throughout, and the taxonomy has no concept slug for the sublime.

holes.name: The Fantastic (Todorov)
holes.what: Todorov's category naming the reader/viewer's sustained hesitation between a natural and a supernatural explanation, bordered by 'the uncanny' and 'the marvelous.'
holes.why: Chapter 18's reading of the Burton-Depp films rests entirely on Todorov's fantastic/uncanny/marvelous scheme, which the taxonomy lacks (Freud's uncanny slug is a different, psychoanalytic concept).
